The Wu page says 'By April 1676, the rebel force possessed 11 provinces'; four of them (Shaanxi, Gansu, Zhejiang, Jiangxi) are drawn as contested, not held (see the ledger).

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: after the surrenders of Geng (1676) and Shang the core is 'Yunnan, Guizhou, Hunan, Guangxi and Sichuan'. Wu proclaimed the Great Zhou at Hengzhou in 1678 and died in October; the Qing then took Yuezhou, Changde and Hengzhou, and in 1680 recovered Hunan, Guizhou, Guangxi and Sichuan, so the shape is soft for 1678-1679.

New keyframe: 'The provinces of Hunan, Guizhou, Guangxi, and Sichuan were recovered by the Qing' in 1680; 'Wu Shifan retreated to Kunming in October'; Kunming fell in October 1681 and he 'committed suicide in December'.

ledger.note: 1673: Wu Sangui rebels in Yunnan. 'Wu killed Zhu Guozhi, the governor of Yunnan, and rebelled' on 28 December 1673; the Revolt page: Wu 'instigated the rebellion' in December 1673. The page does not name Kunming.

1674: Geng Jingzhong rebels in Fujian. 'In 1674 Geng Jingzhong rebelled against Qing rule along with the other two'; he was 'firmly entrenched as a quasi independent ruler in Fujian'. The page is silent on the month and on whether he took orders from Wu: an ally, so the land is drawn with the coalition.
1674: Guizhou. On 7 January 1674 Wu 'took the whole territory of Guizhou province without any loss'.

union.text: Sichuan as the Qing province stood: Sichuan with the Chongqing area

ledger.note: 1674: Hunan, Sichuan and Guangxi. 'By April 1674 ... Wu's army had quickly occupied Hunan, Hubei, Sichuan, and Guangxi'; the Revolt page has 'captured Hunan and Sichuan provinces' (no year) and Sun Yanling rising in Guangxi in 1674. The page's 'by April' is an upper bound; Hubei is on the Wu page alone and is not drawn.
1676: Guangdong. Shang Zhixin 'joined the rebellion, consolidating Guangdong under his rule'. The page gives no month.
1676: Fujian. Geng Jingzhong 'surrendered in 1676'; the Revolt page has Geng and Shang 'surrendered in turn as their forces weakened'. The pages give no month.

1676: the rebels reach into Shaanxi, Gansu, Zhejiang and Jiangxi. 'By April 1676, the rebel force possessed 11 provinces' (Yunnan, Guizhou, Sichuan, Shaanxi, Gansu, Hunan, Guangdong, Guangxi, Fujian, Zhejiang, Jiangxi); the Revolt page has revolts in Shaanxi (Wang Fuchen, 1674) and no other dated hold on these four. They are drawn as contested, not held.

1677: Guangdong returns to the Qing, bridging. Shang Zhixin surrendered after joining in 1676 ('surrendered in turn'); neither page opened gives the year, and the Revolt infobox lists 'Fujian, and Guangdong provinces recovered by Qing'.

1677: the contest over Shaanxi, Gansu, Zhejiang and Jiangxi ends, bridging. Wang Fuchen 'surrendered after a three-year-long stalemate' (his rising was in 1674); no page opened dates the surrender or the end of the rebels' reach in the other three.

1678: Wu Sangui proclaims the Great Zhou. 'In 1678, Wu Sangui went a step further and declared himself the emperor of the "Great Zhou"', era name Zhaowu; the reign began in March 1678 (infobox); he 'established his capital at Hengzhou'. Same state, same colour.
1678: the capital is Hengzhou. 'Established his capital at Hengzhou (present-day Hengyang, Hunan)'; Wu died there on 2 October 1678 (infobox).

region.text: Hengzhou, Changde and Yuezhou in Hunan

ledger.note: 1678: the Qing take Hengzhou, Changde and Yuezhou. After Wu's death the Qing 'captured it, along with the rebel territories of Changde, Hengzhou and others'. The page gives no month; October is the earliest it allows (Wu died on 2 October).

union.text: Sichuan as the Qing province stood: Sichuan with the Chongqing area

ledger.note: 1680: Hunan, Guizhou, Guangxi and Sichuan. 'The provinces of Hunan, Guizhou, Guangxi, and Sichuan were recovered by the Qing' (also 'Sichuan and southern Shaanxi were retaken by the Han Chinese Green Standard Army'). Wu Shifan retreated to Kunming in October.
1681: Kunming and Yunnan. Zhao Liangdong 'was the first to break through into Kunming' in October 1681.

1681: the Zhou ends. 'The remnants of Wu's armies were defeated soon after, in December 1681, and Wu Shifan committed suicide'; the Revolt page: he 'committed suicide in December and the rebels surrendered the following day'.

notes:
Written by ea-07 on 2026-10-25 from three pages (budget 2-5). This is the Revolt of the Three Feudatories as a state: Wu Sangui's Zhou, with Geng Jingzhong's Fujian and Shang Zhixin's Guangdong drawn with it as the coalition (the Geng page: 'along with the other two'; it is silent on whether Geng obeyed Wu). Cliopatria has no row for it: the 'Southern Ming' shapes of 1673 and 1677 are the Revolt, reviewed (verdict wrong, years belong here) in the southern-ming dossier, so cliopatria_names is empty and the five keyframes are new. The qing-dynasty dossier should carry the 1673-1681 gains and losses against this slug, not against southern-ming.

Not settled: what the rebels held in 1674-76 besides the named provinces. The Wu Sangui page says 'By April 1674 ... Hunan, Hubei, Sichuan, and Guangxi' and, 'By April 1676', 11 provinces (adding Shaanxi, Gansu, Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian, Guangdong); the Revolt page names Hunan and Sichuan (no year), Guangxi and Shaanxi risings in 1674, and does not mention Hubei. Hubei is not drawn; Shaanxi, Gansu, Zhejiang and Jiangxi are drawn as a contested zone for 1676, not held (they were reached, not governed, on the pages' own account of Wang Fuchen and Geng). Not dated by any page opened: Shang Zhixin's surrender (the Geng page is silent), the end of the rebels' reach into the north-west, the seat before Hengzhou (1678) and the seat in 1679, and the Revolt infobox's recovery of Yunnan, Fujian and Guangdong (it gives no years). The Tungning landings in Fujian and Guangdong in 1674 are in the kingdom-of-tungning dossier; Taiwan in Cliopatria's 1673 shape is Tungning's and not this state's.

Counterparts: 'qing-dynasty' throughout; the 1673 Cliopatria shape's Guangdong and Fujian cells are in the 1676 and 1674 keyframes here.
